text.content:
An augmentation is an engineered change to a character’s body, which can include their brain (and therefore mind) that grants them some improved or additional ability, that augments them in some way. Cyberpunk is often about the ability to modify and augment body and mind and the effects of doing so on both the individual and society. It’s the “cyber-” part of the genre’s name.

True to the name, many cyberpunk augmentations are cybernetic or bionic, the addition of machine or artificial parts to the body or the replacement of existing body parts with artificial prosthetics, things like cybernetic limbs or sensory organs, even adding computers to the brain and nervous system. This makes the character a cyborg, short for “cybernetic organism,” part biological, part machine. In other instances, augmentations are engineered, but take the form of things like organ transplants, genetic engineering (in vitro or using recombinant DNA and gene-editing), and other biological modifications, sometimes called “wetware” or “biotech.” In some settings, both forms of augmentation are used, although some may show a preference for one over the other.

Body and mind can only be modified so much, at least safely. This is called a character’s Capacity for augmentation. Capacity is measured in slots, which determine the degree to which the character’s body can be modified. Each augmentation “fills” one or more of these slots, up to the character’s total Capacity.

Starting Capacity

The Game Master sets the starting Capacity for player characters in the campaign depending on its style and overall emphasis on augmentation:

  • A low augmentation campaign starts out with default Capacity 0. Characters must improve their Capacity in order to have any augmentations without going over Capacity.
  • A medium augmentation campaign starts out with a default Capacity of 1 or 2. Some augmentation is common, and player characters are all expected to have one or two slots worth to start.
  • A high augmentation campaign starts out with a default Capacity of 3 or even more. Augmentation is all but required for player characters and those willing to trade other benefits to improve their Capacity can have a lot of it.

Starting Capacity slots are effectively “free” and reflect the amount of augmentation player characters are expected to have in the setting. At the Game Master’s discretion, a character can “trade-in” their unused starting Capacity for leveling improvements instead (see Advancement in Chapter 1 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook) but only if you want there to be an incentive for “non-cyber” characters. Otherwise, unused Capacity is simply that: Potential the character hasn’t used yet.

During character creation, a character can improve their Capacity in place or one or more of the benefits granted by

The default in Cyberpunk Slice is that Capacity “belongs” to the character’s mind, and travels with them if they switch bodies, but the number of slots can be influenced by the destination body, like a mixed ability in Chapter 1, though this is normally limited to the bonus slot granted by a synthetic body. Capacity represents a preparedness to accept augmentations not just on a naïve psychological level, but cognitively—the character is training their mind’s “operating system” to accept new input and issue commands beyond their evolutionary (or for AIs, designed) specifications. Beyond that, it’s a game convenience, since players invest advancements in Capacity, and losing them when you switch bodies would be annoying.

However, the Game Master can specify otherwise. This has major effects on characters and the campaign, if body-swapping also occurs. In these games, Capacity slots belong to the body, like a somatic ability. A high-level character with numerous advancements devoted to Capacity slots becomes a target for body thieves, and Capacity probably becomes a purchasable characteristic, though the GM may decide advancements, rather than Resources, better reflect the complex financial costs. In any event, losing your body means losing advancements, unless the GM is charitable enough to return them when your body is considered irrevocably lost. If the GM goes this route, you can re-use your lost advancements on the improvements they were originally destined for (abilities, focuses, and talents) upon gaining a new level.

Remember that all the above applies to Capacity—that is, the potential to take augmentations without Complications (see EXCEEDING CAPACITY)—and not to the augmentations themselves, which fill Capacity slots and stay with whatever body they were installed in.

The Game Master can set a limit on improved starting Capacity for player characters, depending on how prevalent augmentation is in the setting, ranging from 1 (very rare) to 6 or more (quite common).

Improving Capacity

Characters can improve their capacity when leveling (see Advancement in Chapter 1 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook) by trading a leveling improvement for +1 Capacity. The Game Master sets limits on the number of leveling improvements that can be traded for Capacity, typically it is no more than one improvement per level gained, although in a high augmentation campaign it might be two or more.

Exceeding Capacity

Capacity is the amount a character’s body and mind can be modified safely. In many cyberpunk settings, safety is the first thing to go when it comes to getting and maintaining an edge, so characters may choose to add augmentations beyond their capacity, if the GM allows it in the setting. This places a considerable strain on the character’s body or mind, imposing one of the following effects:

  • Ability Reduction: One of the character’s ability scores is reduced by 1 per slot the character is over Capacity. So, the character might suffer a penalty to Strength, Intelligence, Willpower – any ability, so long as it is approved by the GM. The ability affected reflects the type of strain the character is under: Strength is muscle weakness or degradation, Intelligence is loss of cognitive function, and so forth.
  • Breakdown: The strain to the character’s system is such that they suffer a loss of 1d6 + (slots over Capacity) Health per day, every day, so long as they are over Capacity. They can recover this lost Health normally, and

likely spend time and resources doing so on a regular basis. Note that characters can only take a breather (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, p. 46) after an encounter. Characters suffering from breakdown might depend on a lot of medical treatment, possibly including illicit drugs, to maintain some semblance of their normal Health.

  • Complication: Exceeding the character’s capacity causes other problems. The GM receives free stunt points equal to the number of slots over Capacity to impose stunt effects on the character during each adventure. So, a character who is 2 slots over Capacity gives the GM 2 SP they can use for any suitable stunt, such as having the failure of a cybernetic component apply a Knock Prone stunt to the character or a Disarm when the character’s cyber-hand spasms and they drop something. The GM can use complication SP all at once or divide them up among multiple smaller stunts over the course of the adventure. These Complication SP renew at the start of every adventure, so long as the character remains over Capacity.

Characters may be able to mix-and-match different effects from exceeding their Capacity. In any case, the GM should set a reasonable limit on exceeding Capacity, usually a maximum of 6 slots, if this option is allowed at all in the game.

Sample Complications

The following are some examples of Complications Game Masters might introduce based on different SP totals for characters who have exceeded their Capacity. The appropriate Complication(s), like stunts, depend on the circumstances, the character’s augmentations, and the events of the encounter.

General Complications

  • –1 penalty to the character’s next attack roll or ability test per SP spent.
  • –2 penalty to the character’s next damage roll per SP spent.

While Complications—like stunts—are designed to be somewhat random and circumstantial, players and Game Masters can also agree on specific set Complications for over-Capacity characters in a Modern AGE cyberpunk game to suit the character’s particular augmentations and backstory. This has the advantage of both the player and the GM knowing what to expect beforehand and can provide some interesting added details to the character.

Ruby has the augmentations Adrenal Enhancement, Combat Reflexes, Fast Reflexes, and 2 slots of Lightning Reflexes, a total of 6 slots, which is 3 slots over Ruby’s Capacity. Rather than the GM choosing 3 SP worth of Complications for Ruby each adventure, her player suggests a set Complication: When Ruby uses her augmentations in an encounter, after six rounds, she’s incapacitated and must make a TN 15 Willpower (Self-Discipline) test in order to take any actions until she’s had a 5-minute breather. It’s due to the cheap black-market neurotransmitters and biochemicals, which make her sick as a dog after using them, but unbelievably fast and dangerous—for 90 seconds, at least. If Ruby later increases her Capacity, the GM may modify her set Complication, saying she has gotten a better version of her augmentation, or improved her tolerance for using it, or some combination of the two.

  • –1 penalty to the character’s Defense for one turn per SP spent.
  • An opponent gains bonus SP equal to the SP spent, which they can use normally for a stunt against the character.
  • The character is involuntarily moved 2 yards per SP spent.

1-point Complications

  • The character cannot move from where they are for one turn
  • The character loses the use of one augmentation for the next turn as it glitches; augmentations costing more than 1 slot require a Complication equal to their number of slots.

2-point Complications

  • The character falls prone where they are
  • A stun damage attack on the character does wound damage instead
  • An attack on the character ignores half of their Armor Rating
  • An attack on the character does an additional 1d6 damage
  • The character drops whatever they are holding, which lands 1d6 yards away in a direction chosen by the GM
  • The character’s Speed is reduced by 4 for the remainder of the encounter; this complication can be applied multiple times.

3-point Complications

  • The character automatically fails a test or attack roll of the GM’s choice
  • A piece of equipment (not an augmentation) in the character’s possession breaks (jams, overloads, etc.) and cannot be used until it is reset or repaired.
  • The character can take a major or minor action on their next turn, but not both.
  • The character is automatically surprised the next time initiative is rolled for a combat encounter (see Surprise on p. 128 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook).

4-point Complications

  • The character cannot do anything other than free actions for one turn.
  • If the character has less than half their normal Health, they must succeed on a TN 14 Constitution (Stamina) test or immediately fall unconscious.
  • The character drops to the end of the initiative order during an action scene.

5-point Complications

  • A successful attack inflicts an additional 2d6 damage to the character.
  • A successful attack completely ignores the character’s Armor Rating and Toughness.
  • The character must succeed on a TN 15 Constitution (Stamina) test or lose the use of an augmentation chosen by the GM until it can be repaired or replaced.

6-point Complications

  • The character becomes incapable of taking any action, at the end of each of their turns, they can make a TN 15 Willpower (Self-Discipline) test, if they succeed, they shake off the complication and can act normally again on their next turn.
  • The character must succeed on a TN 15 Willpower (Self- Discipline) test or take a random action chosen by the GM on their next turn.
  • If the character has less than half their normal Health, they must succeed on a TN 15 Constitution (Stamina) test, or their condition immediately becomes dying.

Modern AGE characters acquire augmentations in two phases: during character creation and in-play after the campaign has begun. A character who has one or more augmentations is an augment, although different settings may have different— and more colorful—names for it, things like cybered, wired, ‘borg, hacked, juiced, or enhanced, to name a few.

Character Creation Augmentations

Players can fill any Capacity slots available to their characters with augmentations the Game Master says are available in the setting. It is up to the player to develop a suitable backstory for how the character got those augmentations based on the character’s social class, background, and profession, and the nature of the setting. Possibilities may include:

  • A soldier (of any social class) who was augmented for service and allowed to keep the augmentations upon mustering-out—or after deserting and disappearing into the underworld.
  • A criminal augmented by a crime boss or syndicate, who may still hold a debt the character owes.
  • An upper-class character who paid for their own augmentations or had them paid for by family or other wealthy allies.
  • A mega-corporate employee who received their augmentations as a condition or benefit of their employment, past or present.
  • A character (likely low-class) augmented against their will as an experiment or some form of human trafficking.

Encourage players to be creative in terms of detailing the backstory of their characters’ augmentations and offer opportunities in the setting for augments to “go rogue” and become the independent operators players tend to favor in cyberpunk games.

In-Play Augmentations

Acquiring new augmentations in-play requires two things: available Capacity and access to the desired augmentations. The player provides the available Capacity by improving their character’s capacity while leveling (see Improving Capacity, previously), having some previously unused Capacity, or removing an existing augmentation to free up some Capacity. The Game Master generally provides access as part of a reward. This may be a favor or other payment owed to the character, the benefit of a level of Membership, or access granted by a Relationship, to name a few. In essence, it is up to the GM when to green light the ability to fill additional Capacity and what augmentations are available when the character can do so.

Realistically, adding augmentations takes a considerable amount of money to pay for the medical procedures, recovery, and the augmentation itself. This is even more so when the work is done illegally or on the black market. Rather than go through complex formulae to figure out the huge costs of augmentation work, it makes more sense from a campaign perspective to have the Game Master control and provide access. If a player really wants a particular augmentation and their character hasn’t managed to earn means to get it yet, the Game Master can always provide riskier opportunities for the character, like working with a loan-shark or agreeing to take on dangerous (and higher-playing) work for clients who can provide the money or access.

Biological and Synthetic Augmentations

Unless an augmentation specifically involves technological parts or capabilities, such as a built-in radio or computer, the augmentation may be either biological or synthetic in nature, depending on the capabilities of the technology in the setting. Visual augmentations, for example, may involve cloned or surgically altered biological eyes or cybernetic replacements. Whether a particular augmentation is biological or synthetic depends on the type of body the recipient has (see Chapter 1) and whether they want to add biological or synthetic components to it.

Some biological augmentations may be the result of genetic engineering, either in utero encoded into the character’s DNA (for augmentations selected during character creation) or grown in the character through gene-editing, leading to a new phenotype (the expression of a creature’s genetic traits within an environment). These biological augmentations may be inheritable, if the character has offspring, leading to the creation of different sub-species within the campaign setting. Similarly, biological augmentations may result in artificially engineered and grown people with programmed or downloaded memories, who may or may not be legally treated as “real” people.

Cosmetic Alterations

As opposed to augmentations, which improve a character’s abilities, alterations are primarily or entirely “cosmetic” in that they may change the character’s appearance in various ways and may be personally important to the character and their quality of life, but do not provide any game-related enhancements or abilities. Cosmetic alterations have no impact on a character’s Capacity, and merely cost the necessary Resources and access to acquire them. Examples of cosmetic alterations in a Modern AGE cyberpunk setting may include:

  • Body Alteration: Any change to the character’s body that doesn’t affect their game traits. This can be as minor as a permanent change of eye- or hair-color to changing sexual characteristics (making the character a different sex or intersex) or providing scales, skin colors not found in nature (like blue, green, or purple, for example), fiber-optic “hair,” and prosthetic replacement of body parts, including limbs, and other assistive or corrective technology. At the most extreme end, body alteration may involve body replacement with a new cloned or genetically engineered body or a synthetic body (see Biological Bodies and Synthetic Bodies in

Chapter 1) which still don’t count as augmentations unless they change the character’s abilities. The only limits to body alteration are the players’ imaginations, the setting’s available technology, and the requirement they have no in-game benefits.

  • Body Art: These are effectively permanent additions to the character’s appearance, from low-tech tattoos and scarification to more much involved body art, possibly involving light- or heat-activated or even moving inks, and other surgical alterations in appearance. Piercings can fall into this category, although they’re only semi-permanent (depending on their placement and long-term usage) and relatively inexpensive compared to some body art.

A key concept of the cyberpunk genre is the ownership of bodies and the ability to alter them, so players should be encouraged to define their characters’ bodies however they see fit. Cosmetic qualities are widely diverse in a cyberpunk setting and “beauty” is very much in the eye of the beholder (and, possibly, their media “likes” and upvotes), so even cosmetic surgery designed to make a character look especially unusual or to fit a certain ideal aesthetic of beauty shouldn’t be considered a “game benefit” in the campaign.

Augmentations can provide several different game system benefits. The following section outlines the major benefits, how they work, and their relative value in terms of how easy or difficult they are to acquire. The latter is described in numerical “enhancements” (one enhancement, two enhancements, and so on). Note that these benefits are the “bare bones” of augmentation design: The GM should exercise some oversight when it comes to defining augmentations in the game and should feel free to modify the results of these guidelines to best suit the game’s style and setting. The Augmentation Catalog section provides several examples of how you can tweak or modify the basic effects and mechanics to come up with any number of unique augmentations for your game.

Ability

This effect is essentially equivalent to an ability advancement (Modern AGE Basic Rulebook, p. 31) and, for abilities with scores of 5 or less, amounts to a +1 increase to that ability. For higher ability scores, additional enhancements are needed to increase the ability: Abilities from 6 to 8 require two, and abilities from 9 to 13 require three. There’s no real functional difference between an ability enhancement and an ability advancement except the enhancement is artificial and effectively occurs all at once whereas ability advancement reflects practice, training, and experience. Still, it may be a useful effect for certain augmentations.

At the Game Master’s discretion, augmentations can ignore the normal rules for ability advancement, which say the same ability cannot be advanced two levels (or two advancements) in a row. For augmentations, the sole limit is the character’s available slots and Capacity, so someone with 3 available slots could go from a score of 3 in an ability to a score of 6 all at once. It is also up to the Game Master which abilities can be enhanced using augmentations, based on the campaign’s technology. Somatic abilities are the most common, followed by mixed abilities, with augmenting the purely noetic abilities being the most difficult. See Noetic, Somatic, and Mixed Abilities in Chapter 1 for details.

Ability Focus

An effect can grant the benefits of an ability focus, particularly for a somatic ability, or the equivalent of an ability focus—a +2 bonus with tests—for a similarly narrow use of an ability. For example, a bonus on tests to avoid a particular hazard, or to perform a particular task not already covered by an existing focus. In instances where an ability focus enhancement would stack with an existing focus, the combined bonus is considered +3 (rather than +4).

Action

The action effect changes your options for actions on your turn in action time (see Taking Actions in Chapter 2 of the Modern AGE Basic Rulebook).

  • Fast Action: One enhancement lets you take a specific major action as a minor action on your turn. You could, for example, use a type of attack or defend as a minor action. Choose the action when you take the enhancement.
  • Extra Action: One enhancement allows you to take an additional minor action on your turn.
  • Reaction: One enhancement allows you to choose a specific major or minor action and always have it prepared, able to use it with a minor action at any time in reaction to a particular circumstance, even when it is not your turn in the initiative order. You define the action and circumstance when you choose this enhancement.
  • Second Chance: One enhancement allows you to choose a particular ability focus. If you fail an ability test involving that focus, you can re-roll the test and use the result of the second roll.

Characters are limited to a maximum of one major and two minor actions on their turn, even with this enhancement, although they may be able to also perform certain major actions as minor actions.

Defense

This effect grants you either +1 to your Defense or +1 to your Toughness. The GM should set reasonable limits on the additional Defense or Toughness characters can gain, such as a bonus no more than one-third of their level, rounded up. Added Toughness from enhancement provides the usual benefits based on the campaign’s style (gritty, pulpy, or cinematic).

Favored Stunt

Choose a specific stunt available for use in the setting. Each enhancement applied to this effect reduces the stunt’s SP cost for you by 1. If you reduce the stunt’s SP cost to 0, you can perform that stunt at-will whenever there is an opportunity to do so. So, for example, if you have Favored Stunt (Disarm) with two enhancements, any time you hit an armed opponent with a melee attack you can attempt to disarm them, whether you have rolled stunt points or not.

Additionally, you can perform the Activate action for your Favored Stunt, gaining 1 Stunt Point when you do so, much like a use of Stunt Attack. You must perform your Favored Stunt with your next Major Action. (Note, this makes Favored Stunt an expanded version of the Extraordinary Stunt talent in Chapter 11 of Modern AGE.)

Force Multiplier

Choose a particular task largely defined by an ability focus, such as Strength (Jumping) or Intelligence (Research). With one enhancement, you are twice as effective at that task when you succeed in performing it. With two enhancements, you are five times as effective, then ten times, twenty-five, fifty, and finally one hundred times more effective with six enhancements. Examples include:

  • Jumping: Your Force Multiplier affects the distance you can jump with a successful test, from twice as far to a hundred times further than normal!
  • Lifting: Your Force Multiplier increases the amount you can lift, from twice that of someone of your Strength to a hundred times, strong enough to lift a truck over your head!
  • Running: When you take the Run action, your Force Multiplier increases your Speed. It does not affect your Speed for ordinary Move actions during action time, however. At higher multipliers, this enhancement edges into the equivalent of vehicle speeds (see VEHICLE SPEED, p. 76 of Modern AGE). For example, average Speed 10 translates into about 2 mph. At a x25 multiplier, that’s around 50 mph, equal to Fast vehicle speed, while a x100 multiplier is 200 mph or Very Fast speed. These values get even higher with a higher base Speed: A character with Speed 15 and a x100 Running Multiplier tops out around 340 miles per hour!
  • Researching: When you’re reading or otherwise absorbing information, your Force Multiplier increases the amount you can absorb in the same amount of time, from twice as much as normal to a hundred times. In some cases, this may reduce the time interval of advanced tests associated with research, study, or absorbing information, but solely limited to purely mental tasks (see Thinking, following).
  • Thinking: Your Force Multiplier increases the amount you can mentally accomplish same amount of time. Note that this does not change how much you can physically accomplish. While you might be able to solve a complex mathematical equation in your head almost instantly, for example, writing it all out (or explaining it to someone else) would still take some time. Likewise, while you might be able to do engineering design rapidly in your mind, building a prototype would take the usual amount of time. The GM should take this into account for advanced tests: While a Force Multiplier might allow a character to accomplish some elements of an advanced test in a shorter time interval, this only applies to tasks involving pure thought process.

Whereas the Ability enhancement (previously) improves the actual ability score, and therefore benefits tests with that ability, a Force Multiplier improves what you can accomplish with the same ability within a particular defined area.

The campaign’s mode sets limits on Force Multiplier: In Gritty or Pulpy mode, characters are limited to three enhancements (a x10 multiplier), while in Cinematic mode, the limit is six enhancements (a x100 multiplier) unless the GM chooses to set a lower limit.

Hazard Immunity

Choose a particular type of environmental hazard. For a number of enhancements equal to the hazard’s category—one for minor, two for moderate, and so on—you are essentially immune to that hazard. See Hazards in Chapter 8 of Modern AGE for details. Common examples include immunity to drowning (essentially, the ability to breathe underwater) or a short (10-foot) fall for one enhancement, immunity to suffocation or a longer fall for two enhancements, immunity to environmental cold or heat, or to diseases or toxins (ranging from two to four enhancements), or immunity to exposure to radiation or the hard vacuum of space, for five or six enhancements.

As with Force Multiplier, the GM may want to set limits on Hazard Immunity based on mode: one or two enhancements for Gritty, no more than three enhancements for Pulpy campaigns, and up to six for Cinematic campaigns.

Innate Attack

You have some sort of innate damaging attack beyond just a person’s usual unarmed abilities. With once enhancement, your innate attack does 1d6 damage in close combat. Each additional enhancement increases its damage by 1d6, to a maximum of 4d6.

Choose whether your innate attack causes Impact or Ballistic damage and Stun or Wound damage. Choose an ability and focus you use for your attack roll with the Innate Attack, such as Fighting (Brawling) or Accuracy (Pistols). At the GM’s discretion, you may have a special focus for this attack replace another of your ability focuses. You may also choose an ability score to add to your innate attack’s damage, either Strength, Dexterity, or Perception. These choices do not change once they are made. If you have talents which confer damage bonuses, they may apply to your Innate Attack provided it is of the appropriate type. For example, an “unarmed” damage bonus might apply to an Innate Attack involving claws or steel-hard fists. Consult the GM in cases where it is not clear whether a bonus should apply.

For an additional enhancement, your innate attack can be used at range, with a range of 50 yards. A second enhancement doubles this range to 100 yards. Finally, for a separate additional enhancement, your innate attack can cause Penetrating damage, but you must halve the damage after it is rolled, rounding up.

Innate Power

Choose a specific power from the extraordinary powers given in Chapter 6 of Modern AGE or in Chapters 1 and 2 of this book. You can use that power as if you possessed the appropriate degree of its talent and you can learn the ability focus associated with that power’s talent. It takes one enhancement for a Novice power, two for an Expert power, and three for a Master power, and you do not have to have the lower degree powers: You can simply have a Master power and nothing else, for example. If the possessor of an Innate Power does not already have a Power Points score, they gain one upon acquiring the power, the same as a character wielding an extraordinary power (see Modern AGE, Chapter 6, for details).

In most cyberpunk campaigns, this effect of augmentations is limited to things that can be simulated or duplicated by technology. So, for example, Digital Arcana may be available as, essentially, “wireless hacking” capabilities of a computer-brain implant, but Healing Arcana isn’t likely unless there are biological nano-machines capable of instantly repairing wounds, and Power Arcana doesn’t do anything, if there isn’t any magic for it to affect. If there are extraordinary powers other than augmentations in the setting, then it is up to the GM whether augmentations can duplicate them: It’s quite possible there are enchanted implants, spellcasting programs, or brain-modifications that duplicate psychic powers, for examples, in setting that allow for them.

Special Stunt

Create a special or unique stunt, one that does not exist in the Modern AGE rulebook. As an enhancement, your character can perform this new stunt at its normal stunt point cost. The information and guidelines in Chapter 4 of the Modern AGE Companion may be useful in coming up with new stunts, and you can base them off the examples of existing stunts. Often a special stunt implies or relies on capabilities ordinary people do not have, such as a Taser Punch stunt, allowing you to generate a burst of electricity and inflict an additional 1d6 Penetrating electrical damage with a successful unarmed strike for 2 stunt points. The GM should approve the final SP cost and mechanics of the new stunt. Special stunts are useful for augmentations that have unpredictable or variable effects or that do not always come into play, but function more like regular stunts.

You can apply the benefits of the Favored Stunt effect (previously) to a Special Stunt, reducing its SP cost. If it is reduced to 0, you can perform the Special Stunt at-will whenever there is an opportunity to do so, the same as with a regular Favored Stunt.

Perquisite

As an enhancement, you gain a single specific benefit or advantage (a perquisite or “perk”) that’s useful but does not otherwise conform to the benefits given previously. Perquisites can be almost anything the player and GM can agree upon, from the ability to project a beam of light equivalent to a flashlight at will to malleable facial features giving you the benefit of always having a “disguise kit” or an implanted cellular communicator. A good guideline for a perquisite is the innate benefit of a minor piece of equipment or the like. The Game Master may rule that some perquisites require more than one enhancement, particularly if they are multi-functional or have broad benefits.

Enhancement Limits

Just as the Game Master can decide whether to allow extraordinary abilities in the game at all, the GM can also set limits on the benefits available from enhancements, ranging from no more than X enhancements spent on a particular benefit (say 1–3) or no Innate Attack or Innate Power enhancements, no reducing stunt point costs below 1, or any other guidelines the GM wishes to establish. Just because an enhancement is potentially possible in the context of the game rules does not mean a player has to have to option to acquire it for their character in a particular campaign. As always, the needs and the design of the setting take precedence.
